newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cattle on feed numbers seen close to year ago.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cattle on feed numbers seen close to year ago.

text.p: U.S. cattle feeders, heartened by profitable margins and sliding feed prices, increasingly placed cattle in feedlots this fall, a trend expected to be borne out by U.S. Agriculture Department data on Friday.
The USDA is expected to report that the number of cattle on feed in major feedlots continued to rise during October and as of November 1, approached year-ago levels, analysts said.

The average of analysts' estimates for cattle on feed in feedlots with 1,000-head or more capacity in the seven primary states as of November 1 was 99.5 percent of a year ago, in a range of 97.6 to 100.5 percent.
"There is incentive enough, with the grain prices continuing to come down, to keep placing (cattle)" onto feedlots, said Dan Vaught, analyst with AG Edwards in St. Louis, Mo.

USDA will release its monthly Cattle on Feed report at 1400 CST Friday. This is the eleventh time for the 12-state report, but analysts continue to only estimate data for feedlots in the seven key states with capacities of 1,000 head or more as historical data continues to build.

Marketing estimates for October were down from a year ago, ranging from 95.5 to 100 percent of last year and averaging 97.3 percent. October marketings were expected to be down despite one more marketing day in the period this year than last.
The reduced shipments of feedlot cattle were partly attributed to cattle moving directly from grazing to slaughter and bypassing inclusion in feedlot marketing numbers for the month.

"I think there are a lot of heavy feeders being slaughtered, going from pasture at 900 to 1,000 lbs straight to slaughter. That is one reason why you have seen the marketings figure come in a lot below the slaughter steer and heifer" data from the USDA," Vaught said.

Low cattle prices last year encouraged owners to keep feeder cattle on pasture longer. In some cases they were too heavy to put on feed and still grade choice, so they went directly to slaughter, Vaught added.
